did_you_know.text: Did you know? The book of Obadiah opens with a proclamation about a messenger sent to the nations, calling them to gather for war against Edom.
Did you know? Edom is described as a small and despised nation among the nations, even though its heart is filled with pride and self-confidence.

Did you know? According to the prophecy, Edom’s pride comes from living in the “clefts of the rock”—rocky ravines and mountain strongholds—which led it to think that no one could bring it down from its position.

Did you know? The prophet compares Edom’s destruction to robbery and grape harvesting: even if thieves or grape gatherers came, they would normally leave something behind; but Edom’s destruction is described as more complete.
Did you know? The prophecy portrays Esau as being searched out so that all his hidden treasures will be exposed—in other words, his wealth and secrets will not remain concealed.
Did you know? Edom’s allies are described as deceiving it and even turning its bread into a trap; the prophecy thus emphasizes that its alliances will not save it.
Did you know? The main reason for Edom’s punishment is the “violence” it committed against Jacob: standing by while Judah was in distress and harming its brother in the time of his downfall.

Did you know? The message about the day of the Lord is not limited to Edom: it is described as a day soon to come upon all the nations, when people will be treated as they have treated others—“your deeds will return upon your own head.”

Did you know? Alongside the judgment of Edom, the prophecy promises that there will be survivors on Mount Zion and that it will be a holy place; the house of Jacob will return and take possession of its inheritance.

Did you know? The book concludes by placing ultimate sovereignty in the hands of the Lord: deliverers will go up from Mount Zion to judge the mountain of Esau, and then it states explicitly, “the kingdom shall be the Lord’s.”
